calc.mortgage.title: Mortgage Calculator
calc.mortgage.desc: Work out the monthly payment on a home loan and what it costs in total.
calc.mortgage.note: Property tax, insurance, fees and any rate reset during the term are not included.
calc.mortgage.explain: The payment is level for the whole term. Early payments are mostly interest, and the share going to the principal grows every month - the breakdown table shows exactly when that crosses over for your figures.
calc.auto-loan.title: Auto Loan Calculator
calc.auto-loan.desc: Calculate the monthly payment and total interest on a car loan.
calc.auto-loan.explain: A larger down payment cuts both the amount borrowed and the interest charged on it. Shorter terms raise the monthly payment but lower the total cost.
calc.loan.title: Loan Calculator
calc.loan.desc: Monthly payment, total interest and payoff schedule for any loan.
calc.loan.explain: Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, which falls a little with every payment. The level payment splits differently each month as a result.
calc.loan.faq.1.q: Does paying extra reduce the interest?
calc.loan.faq.1.a: Yes. Anything paid above the scheduled amount goes straight to the principal, which cuts both the balance and all the interest that would have accrued on it.
calc.loan.faq.2.q: Why does the interest barely fall in the first years?
calc.loan.faq.2.a: Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, which is at its highest at the start. The breakdown table shows the crossover year for your figures.
calc.loan.faq.3.q: How does the interest rate affect my payment?
calc.loan.faq.3.a: A higher rate raises both the monthly payment and the total interest, because each month's interest is a share of the outstanding balance. The longer the loan, the bigger the effect, since the rate applies for more months.
calc.loan.faq.4.q: How does the loan term affect the total interest?
calc.loan.faq.4.a: A longer term lowers the monthly payment but raises the total interest, because the balance is paid down more slowly and interest is charged on it for longer. A shorter term costs more each month and less overall.
calc.loan.faq.5.q: Can I use this calculator in a different currency?
calc.loan.faq.5.a: Yes. Select a country to change currency, number formatting and input ranges. Starting rates are illustrative assumptions, not current lender offers. Replace them with your quoted rate. The same repayment formula is used; selecting a country does not model its lending laws, fees or borrower eligibility.
calc.loan.faq.6.q: What is the difference between principal and interest?
calc.loan.faq.6.a: The principal is the amount you borrowed; the interest is what the lender charges for it. Each payment covers that month's interest first and the rest reduces the principal, so the split shifts towards principal over the life of the loan.
calc.student-loan.title: Student Loan Calculator
calc.student-loan.desc: See what a student loan costs to repay and how long it takes.
calc.student-loan.explain: This treats the loan as a fixed repayment plan. Income-linked repayments, forgiveness and write-off rules depend on the scheme and are not modeled here.
calc.student-loan.note.generic: Assumes a fixed repayment schedule at a constant rate.
calc.student-loan.note.incomeContingent: Repayments here are income-contingent in practice: you pay a share of earnings above a threshold, not a fixed instalment, and the balance is written off after the statutory period.
calc.income-tax.title: Income Tax Calculator
calc.income-tax.desc: Estimate the tax on your annual income and what you keep after it.
calc.income-tax.explain.1: Income is reduced by the allowances and deductions you qualify for, then the remainder is taxed band by band - each rate applies only to the income inside its own band.
calc.income-tax.explain.2: The effective rate is total tax over gross income. The marginal rate is what the next unit of income would be taxed at.
calc.income-tax.faq.1.q: Why is my effective rate lower than my band rate?
calc.income-tax.faq.1.a: Because only the income above each threshold is taxed at that band's rate. The income below it is taxed at the lower rates, so the average always lands under the top rate you reach.
calc.income-tax.faq.2.a: No. This covers the main allowances and the standard deduction. Special reliefs, credits and local taxes are not modelled, so treat the result as an estimate.

calc.vat.title: {tax} Calculator
calc.vat.desc: Add or remove {tax} from any amount and see the split.
calc.vat.explain: On a tax-exclusive amount the tax is added on top. On a tax-inclusive amount it is worked back out, which is why dividing by the rate is not the same as multiplying by it.
calc.vat.faq.1.q: How do I get the pre-tax price from a final price?
calc.vat.faq.1.a: Switch the amount type to “Tax already included”. The calculator divides by one plus the rate, which is the only correct way to reverse it.
calc.vat.note.in: Within a state GST splits equally into CGST and SGST; across states the same total is charged as IGST.
calc.vat.note.us: Sales tax rates are set by state, county and city, so pick the rate that applies where the sale happens.
calc.vat.note.gb: The standard rate is 20%. Some goods are reduced-rated at 5% and others, including most food and children's clothing, are zero-rated.
calc.vat.note.ca: GST alone is 5%. HST provinces combine it with the provincial share into a single rate, and others charge PST or QST separately.

calc.capital-gains.title: Capital Gains Tax Calculator
calc.capital-gains.desc: Estimate the tax on an investment gain and what you keep.
calc.capital-gains.explain: The gain is the sale price less what you paid. How it is taxed depends on how long you held the asset and, in several countries, on the rest of your income.
calc.capital-gains.note.us: Long-term rates apply after twelve months; shorter holdings are taxed as ordinary income. The 3.8% net investment income tax is not included.
calc.capital-gains.note.gb: UK 2026/27 resident individual ordinary chargeable gains only, assuming the full £3,000 annual exemption is unused elsewhere. Enter adjusted acquisition cost and net disposal proceeds after eligible costs. Taxable gains fill the unused £37,700 basic-rate band above your entered taxable income at 18%, then 24%. Holding duration does not change these rates. Excludes FIG/OWR claims, carried interest, business relief, losses, share matching, joint ownership allocation and exempt assets. This is not total annual liability or a reporting/deadline check.
calc.capital-gains.note.ca: Half the gain is taxable and added to income. The marginal rate used here is indicative and excludes provincial tax.
calc.capital-gains.note.au: Assets held over twelve months qualify for the 50% discount; the remainder is taxed at your marginal rate.
calc.capital-gains.note.de: Germany 2026, resident single private investor with ordinary taxable securities acquired after 2008 and no church tax. Enter adjusted acquisition cost, net disposal proceeds and the unused portion of your €1,000 saver allowance; zero means already used. Positive gain after this allowance is taxed at 25% plus solidarity surcharge of 5.5% of that tax (26.375% combined), regardless of holding time. Excludes losses, funds/partial exemptions, property, crypto, business/substantial holdings, joint assessment and foreign-tax credits. A lower-rate election may reduce actual liability; not calculated here. No refund or loss relief is calculated. This is a flat-rate illustration:26.375% applies before rounding. The25% income-tax component is displayed rounded to the nearest cent; solidarity is5.5% of the unrounded component with fractional cents discarded, then the displayed components are added. Bank withholding and final tax-assessment rounding are not modeled.
calc.capital-gains.note.fr: France: 2025 ordinary private securities gains assessed in 2026, single resident with full French social levies, default PFU only. Positive net proceeds minus adjusted cost: 12.8% income tax plus 18.6% social levies, regardless of holding time. Enter the higher total CEHR/CDHR reference income including the gain, up to €250,000. No progressive election, losses/carryforwards, PEA or employee schemes, special reliefs, foreign credits, crypto, property or business gains. Not for foreign social affiliation or high-income assessments. Estimate before collection thresholds and whole-return rounding; no refund or filing calculation.
calc.capital-gains.note.es: Spain 2026: ordinary resident in common territory, taxable savings-base gains. Enter adjusted acquisition cost, net disposal proceeds and other taxable savings income, not salary. Positive gain stacks above that savings base at 19%, 21%, 23%, 27% and 30%, with boundaries €6,000/50,000/200,000/300,000; holding time is irrelevant. Assumes the personal/family minimum is fully absorbed by the general base. Excludes loss offsets, minimum allocation, joint reductions, Basque/Navarre, Ceuta/Melilla, special exemptions and foreign-tax credits. Not a full return; no loss/refund calculation.
calc.capital-gains.note.it: Italy 2025: resident private individual, ordinary taxable securities gains within the 26% substitute-tax regime only. Enter adjusted acquisition cost and net disposal proceeds. A positive gain is taxed at 26% regardless of holding time. No loss offsets/carryforwards, preferential government bonds, funds, crypto, property, business or special holdings, foreign-tax credits, filing or payment calculation. A negative difference produces zero estimated tax, not a loss-relief or refund calculation.
calc.capital-gains.note.in: Listed equity held over twelve months is taxed at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh of gains; shorter holdings are taxed at 20%.
calc.stamp-duty.title: Stamp Duty Calculator
calc.stamp-duty.desc: Work out the stamp duty land tax on a property purchase.
calc.stamp-duty.explain: Stamp duty is banded like income tax: each rate applies only to the slice of the price inside its band, so the effective rate is always lower than the top band you reach.
calc.stamp-duty.note: England and Northern Ireland residential SDLT from 1 April 2025, not Wales or Scotland. Includes standard bands, declared first-time relief up to £500,000, 5 percentage points for additional property and an optional 2 points for non-UK residents. You must establish buyer/relief/residency eligibility. Excludes linked transactions, lease rent, corporate buyers and special reliefs. The table shows base bands; surcharges are separate.
calc.church-tax.title: Church Tax Calculator
calc.church-tax.desc: Estimate the church tax charged alongside your income tax.
calc.church-tax.explain: Church tax is charged as a percentage of your income tax, not of your income, so it rises and falls with the tax bill rather than with earnings.
calc.church-tax.note: 8% in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, 9% in the other federal states. Leaving the church formally ends the liability.
calc.property-tax.title: Property Tax Calculator
calc.property-tax.desc: Multiply a taxable assessed value by the annual property-tax rate you enter.
calc.property-tax.explain: Enter the taxable assessed value after applicable assessment adjustments and exemptions, and the annual percentage from your local authority. Zero percent is an editable placeholder, not an exemption. Annual amount = value × rate / 100; monthly amount = annual / 12; ten-year amount assumes both inputs stay unchanged. Example: 200,000 at 1.25% gives 2,500 per year. This does not value a property, supply local rates, decide eligibility, calculate credits or add fixed levies. Market price may differ from taxable assessed value. Country changes currency only.

calc.retirement.title: Retirement Calculator
calc.retirement.desc: See what your savings could grow to by the time you retire.
calc.retirement.explain: Existing savings and future contributions are projected forward at the expected return, then discounted by inflation to show what the total would actually buy.
calc.retirement.todayHint: What that amount would buy at today's prices.
calc.pension.title: Pension Calculator
calc.pension.desc: Project your pension pot from your own and your employer's contributions.
calc.pension.explain: This is a private savings illustration using your salary, employee/employer contribution percentages and a constant return. Default percentages are examples, not legal minimums or employer commitments. It does not calculate a state pension, eligibility, statutory limits, tax relief or fees. Salary and contributions are constant; returns and inflation can change. The displayed 4% withdrawal is only a scenario, not guaranteed sustainable income.

calc.401k.title: 401(k) Calculator
calc.401k.desc: Project your 401(k) balance, including the employer match.
calc.401k.explain: The employer match is the highest-return part of the plan: contributing at least up to the match limit takes the full amount on offer.
calc.401k.note: Uses the 2026 elective deferral limit of $24,500. Catch-up contributions from age 50 are not included.
calc.social-security-benefit.title: Social Security Benefits Calculator
calc.social-security-benefit.desc: Estimate your monthly Social Security retirement benefit.
calc.social-security-benefit.explain: 2026 first-eligibility cohort (age 62 in 2026), full retirement age 67. Enter 12 times your already established average indexed monthly earnings, not current salary. Two bend points: $1,286 and $7,749; three rates: 90%, 32%, 15%. AIME is rounded down to dollars, PIA to dimes, adjusted monthly benefit to dollars. Ages 62/65/67/70 compare claiming factors in constant 2026 values, excluding later COLAs. No earnings-record indexing, eligibility determination, earnings test, family benefits, Medicare deductions or income tax. This is an illustration, not an SSA award.

calc.superannuation.title: Superannuation Calculator
calc.superannuation.desc: Project your super balance from employer and extra contributions.
calc.superannuation.explain: Employer contributions go in at the Superannuation Guarantee rate and are taxed at 15% on the way in. What is left compounds until retirement.
calc.superannuation.note: Uses the 12% Superannuation Guarantee rate from 1 July 2025. Contribution caps and Division 293 tax are not modelled.
calc.hecs.title: HECS-HELP Calculator
calc.hecs.desc: See what your HELP debt costs each year and when it clears.
calc.hecs.explain: HELP repayments are compulsory once income passes the threshold and are taken as a share of earnings. The debt is indexed each year, so repayments race indexation.
calc.hecs.note: Uses the selected {year} ATO repayment table. Enter repayment income, not salary alone: taxable income excluding assessable FHSS releases, reportable fringe benefits, net investment losses, reportable super contributions and exempt foreign employment income. Enter the current debt after any applicable debt reduction. The projection holds the selected table fixed, applies your indexation before repayment, floors each projected income to whole AUD and rounds annual repayments to cents. Future thresholds, actual indexation dates, eligibility, assessment rounding and refunds are not calculated.
calc.social-security.title: Social Security Contributions Calculator
calc.social-security.desc: See the social contributions taken from your salary.
calc.social-security.explain: Contributions are charged on gross pay, often only up to a ceiling, and fund pensions, healthcare and unemployment cover. They are separate from income tax.
calc.social-security.note: Employee contributions only. Employer contributions are charged on top and are not shown here.
calc.national-insurance.title: National Insurance Calculator
calc.national-insurance.desc: Work out the National Insurance due on your earnings.
calc.national-insurance.explain: Class 1 National Insurance is charged at 8% on earnings between the primary threshold and the upper earnings limit, then at 2% above it.
calc.national-insurance.note: 2026/27 annualised category A employee Class 1 NI: 8% above £12,570 to £50,270, then 2%. Assumes a full year and eligibility to pay. Employer NI, age exemptions, other categories, multiple employments and pay-period rounding are excluded. Monthly values are annual totals divided by 12, not exact payroll deductions.
calc.cpp.title: CPP Calculator
calc.cpp.desc: Calculate your Canada Pension Plan contributions.
calc.cpp.explain: Contributions run at 5.95% on earnings between the basic exemption and the year's maximum pensionable earnings, with a second tier above that.
calc.cpp.note: Scope: 2026 full-year employee CPP including CPP2 and EI outside Quebec, using annual pensionable/insurable earnings. It excludes QPP/QPIP, self-employment, employer contributions, partial years, age exemptions and pay-period rounding. Monthly amounts are annual totals divided by 12, not payslip withholding. Use CRA guidance for your employment situation.
calc.ei.title: EI Calculator
calc.ei.explain: EI premiums are charged at a flat rate on insurable earnings up to the annual maximum, after which nothing further is due for the year.
calc.ei.note: Scope: 2026 full-year employee CPP including CPP2 and EI outside Quebec, using annual pensionable/insurable earnings. It excludes QPP/QPIP, self-employment, employer contributions, partial years, age exemptions and pay-period rounding. Monthly amounts are annual totals divided by 12, not payslip withholding. Use CRA guidance for your employment situation.
calc.30-percent-ruling.title: 30% Ruling Calculator
calc.30-percent-ruling.desc: See what the Dutch 30% ruling is worth to you each year.
calc.30-percent-ruling.explain: Under the ruling part of your salary is paid free of tax, which cuts your taxable income and moves the rest into lower brackets. The benefit is the difference in net pay.
calc.30-percent-ruling.note: Netherlands 2026: assumes an approved ruling and employer agreement for the full year, the WNT cap applies, resident below AOW age with full national insurance, wages only. Enter the annual package including the allowance. Maximum tax-free amount is the lowest of 30% of the package, €78,600 and the amount leaving taxable wages strictly above €48,013 (or €36,497 for qualifying master’s graduates under 30 throughout the year). No 27% rate applies to this 2026 calculation. Excludes eligibility assessment, partial years, turning 30, pre-cap grandfathering, researchers/doctors, actual-cost election, Box 2/3 and pension/health deductions. Benefit compares modelled annual taxes/credits, not payslip withholding or guaranteed pay.
calc.payroll.title: Payroll Calculator
calc.payroll.desc: See the full cost of employing someone, from gross pay to employer charges.
calc.payroll.explain: The employer pays more than the gross salary: social charges sit on top, while tax and employee contributions come out of the gross to give take-home pay.
calc.payroll.note: Employer charges here are indicative averages. Actual rates depend on sector, headcount and insurance choices.
calc.severance-pay.title: Severance Pay Calculator
calc.severance-pay.desc: Calculate severance and notice pay under Turkish labour law.
calc.severance-pay.explain: Türkiye, ordinary eligible severance with at least one year of service. Select the half-year of termination (2025/2026); its ceiling applies to monthly gross remuneration including regular benefits. Gross severance = capped monthly remuneration × decimal service years; stamp duty is 0.759%. Enter the eligible service fraction yourself; this tool does not establish entitlement, dates, breaks or special-contract treatment. Notice pay is a separate gross illustration: monthly remuneration / 30 × 28 days up to 1.5 years, 42 days up to 3 years, then 56 days. It is not automatically due, is not added to the main result and excludes notice income tax and stamp duty. Check contractual terms and legal eligibility.
calc.severance-pay.capHint: The statutory ceiling per year of service.
calc.severance-pay.note: Türkiye, ordinary eligible severance with at least one year of service. Enter the eligible service fraction yourself; this tool does not establish entitlement, dates, breaks or special-contract treatment. calc.tip.title: Tip Calculator
calc.tip.desc: Split a bill and work out the tip per person.
calc.tip.explain: The tip is a percentage of the bill before it is divided, so everyone contributes the same share of both.
calc.inflation.title: Inflation Calculator
calc.inflation.desc: See what an amount will cost later, or what it is worth today.
calc.inflation.explain: Inflation compounds: a steady rate has a small effect over a year and a large one over a decade, which is why long-horizon plans have to account for it.
calc.sip.title: SIP Calculator
calc.sip.desc: See what a fixed monthly investment could grow into over time.
calc.sip.stepUpHint: Raise the instalment by this much every year.
calc.sip.explain.1: Each instalment is invested at the start of the month and compounds monthly at the expected rate, so early instalments do the heaviest lifting.

conv.pair.desc: Convert {from} to {to}, with the conversion factor and a quick reference table.
conv.length.title: Length Converter
conv.length.desc: Convert between metric and imperial lengths.
conv.length.explain: Every length here is defined against the metre. The imperial units are exact conversions rather than approximations: an inch is defined as 25.4 mm, which makes a foot exactly 0.3048 m.
conv.weight.title: Weight Converter
conv.weight.desc: Convert between grams, kilograms, pounds, ounces and stone.
conv.weight.explain: These are units of mass rather than weight in the physics sense. The pound is defined as exactly 0.45359237 kg, so conversions between the metric and imperial units are exact.
conv.temperature.title: Temperature Converter
conv.temperature.desc: Convert between Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin.
conv.temperature.explain: Temperature conversion needs more than a scale factor: Celsius and Fahrenheit have different zero points, so their conversion uses an offset as well as multiplication.
conv.area.title: Area Converter
conv.area.desc: Convert between square metres, feet, acres and hectares.
conv.area.explain: Area units are the square of their length units, which is why the factors are larger than people expect: a square foot is about a tenth of a square metre, not a third.
conv.volume.title: Volume Converter
conv.volume.desc: Convert between litres, millilitres, gallons and cups.
conv.volume.explain: US and imperial gallons are different sizes - an imperial gallon is about 20% larger - so a recipe or fuel figure is only meaningful once you know which one it used.
conv.speed.title: Speed Converter
conv.speed.desc: Convert between km/h, mph, m/s and knots.
conv.speed.explain: All of these are a distance divided by a time, so converting between them is just converting the distance and the time separately.
conv.data.title: Data Converter
conv.data.desc: Convert between bytes, kilobytes, megabytes and their binary equivalents.
conv.data.explain: Decimal prefixes count in thousands and binary prefixes in 1024s. A gigabyte and a gibibyte are not the same size, which is why a drive sold as 1 TB shows up as about 931 GiB.
conv.time.title: Time Converter
conv.time.desc: Convert between seconds, minutes, hours, days and years.
conv.time.explain: Months and years vary in length, so those two use the average Gregorian year of 365.2425 days. Anything shorter than a month converts exactly.
conv.energy.title: Energy Converter
conv.energy.desc: Convert between joules, calories, kilowatt-hours and BTU.
conv.energy.explain: The calorie on food labels is a kilocalorie - a thousand of the calories used in physics. Both appear here, so check which one your figure is in.
conv.pressure.title: Pressure Converter
conv.pressure.desc: Convert between bar, psi, pascals and atmospheres.
conv.pressure.explain: These are all force over area. Tyre pressures are usually quoted as gauge pressure, which is measured relative to the surrounding air rather than to a vacuum.
conv.power.title: Power Converter
conv.power.desc: Convert between watts, kilowatts and horsepower.
conv.power.explain: Mechanical horsepower and metric horsepower differ by about 1.4%, which is why the same engine is quoted at slightly different numbers in different markets.
conv.angle.title: Angle Converter
conv.angle.desc: Convert between degrees, radians and gradians.
conv.angle.explain: A full turn is 360 degrees, 2π radians or 400 gradians. Radians are the natural unit in maths because the arc length of a unit circle equals the angle.
conv.fuel-economy.title: Fuel Economy Converter
conv.fuel-economy.desc: Convert between L/100 km, mpg and km/L.
conv.fuel-economy.explain: L/100 km measures consumption and mpg measures economy, so they run in opposite directions: a lower L/100 km is better, a higher mpg is better. Converting between them means taking a reciprocal, not multiplying.

tool.date-difference.title: Date Difference Calculator
tool.date-difference.desc: Count the days, weeks and working days between two dates.
tool.date-difference.explain: The difference is counted in whole days in UTC. Using local time would make the answer wrong across a daylight-saving change, where two dates can be 23 or 25 hours apart.
tool.add-days.title: Add or Subtract Days
tool.add-days.desc: Find the date a number of days, weeks or months away.
tool.add-days.explain: Adding months clamps rather than rolls over: one month after 31 January is 28 February, not 3 March. Adding days and weeks is exact.
tool.working-days.title: Working Days Calculator
tool.working-days.desc: Count business days between two dates, excluding weekends.
tool.working-days.explain: Saturdays and Sundays are excluded and both endpoints are counted. Public holidays vary by country and region, so they are yours to subtract rather than assumed.
tool.age.title: Age Calculator
tool.age.desc: Work out an exact age in years, months and days.
tool.age.explain: Age is counted in calendar terms rather than by dividing days by 365.25, so it matches the way birthdays actually work, including across leap years.
tool.week-number.title: Week Number Calculator
tool.week-number.desc: Find the ISO week number for any date.
tool.week-number.explain: ISO 8601 weeks start on Monday, and week 1 is the week containing 4 January. That is why the first days of January sometimes fall in week 52 or 53 of the previous year.
tool.percentage.title: Percentage Calculator
tool.percentage.desc: Percentage of a value, share, change and increases.
tool.percentage.explain: Four different questions get asked as “percentage”, and they have different formulas. Picking the right one first is most of the work.
tool.number-to-words.title: Number to Words
tool.number-to-words.desc: Spell a number out, the way an amount is written on a cheque.
tool.number-to-words.explain: Numbers are spelled using the short scale, where a billion is a thousand million, and hundreds are joined with “and” in the British style.
tool.roman-numerals.title: Roman Numeral Converter
tool.roman-numerals.desc: Convert numbers to Roman numerals and back.
tool.roman-numerals.explain: Standard subtractive notation is used, so 9 is IX rather than VIIII. Input is checked by converting it back: IIII and IC are rejected as malformed rather than guessed at.
tool.prime-checker.title: Prime Number Checker
tool.prime-checker.desc: Check whether a number is prime and see its factors.
tool.prime-checker.explain: Divisors are tested only up to the square root: any factor above it pairs with one below, so there is nothing left to find beyond that point.
tool.fraction-simplifier.title: Fraction Simplifier
tool.fraction-simplifier.desc: Reduce a fraction and see it as a decimal and a percentage.
tool.fraction-simplifier.explain: A fraction is reduced by dividing both parts by their greatest common divisor, which is found with the Euclidean algorithm.
tool.random-number.title: Random Number Generator
tool.random-number.desc: Draw random numbers in a range, with or without repeats.
tool.random-number.explain: Numbers come from the browser's cryptographic generator, and draws outside a whole multiple of the range are discarded. Taking a simple remainder would make the lowest numbers slightly more likely.
tool.password-generator.title: Password Generator
tool.password-generator.desc: Generate a strong random password in your browser.
tool.password-generator.explain: Characters are drawn uniformly from the sets you enable. Look-alike characters such as l, I, 1, O and 0 are left out, because a password you cannot read back is a password you will write down.
tool.savings-goal.title: Savings Goal Planner
tool.savings-goal.desc: See how long a savings target takes, and what it takes to hit a date.
tool.savings-goal.explain: Interest compounds monthly on the running balance, including the deposits already made. The answer is how long the target takes at that deposit, and what deposit would reach it by your chosen month.
tool.debt-payoff.title: Debt Payoff Planner
tool.debt-payoff.desc: See how long a debt takes to clear and what the interest costs.
tool.debt-payoff.explain: Interest is charged on the outstanding balance each month before the payment is applied. If the payment is smaller than that interest the balance grows, and the planner says so rather than returning a number.

chart.col.name: Name
chart.length.title: Length Conversion Table
chart.length.desc: Metres, centimetres, feet, inches and yards side by side.
chart.length.explain: Every value is computed from the exact definitions - an inch is 25.4 mm by definition, not by measurement - so the table agrees with the converter to the last decimal shown.
chart.weight.title: Weight Conversion Table
chart.weight.desc: Kilograms, pounds, grams, ounces and stone side by side.
chart.weight.explain: These are units of mass. The pound is defined as exactly 0.45359237 kg, so the metric and imperial columns are exact conversions rather than approximations.
chart.temperature.title: Temperature Conversion Table
chart.temperature.desc: Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin at the temperatures people look up.
chart.temperature.explain: Temperature conversions need an offset as well as a scale, which is why the columns do not stay in a fixed ratio the way length or weight do.
chart.area.title: Area Conversion Table
chart.area.desc: Square metres, square feet, yards, acres and hectares.
chart.area.explain: Area factors are the square of the length factors, which is why a square foot is about a tenth of a square metre rather than a third.
chart.volume.title: Volume Conversion Table
chart.volume.desc: Litres, millilitres, gallons and cups side by side.
chart.volume.explain: US and imperial gallons are different sizes, so both appear here. A recipe or fuel figure means different things depending on which one it used.
chart.speed.title: Speed Conversion Table
chart.speed.desc: km/h, mph, m/s and knots at common speeds.
chart.speed.explain: Every entry is a distance over a time, so converting between them is converting the distance and the time separately.
chart.pressure.title: Pressure Conversion Table
chart.pressure.desc: Bar, psi, kilopascals and atmospheres side by side.
chart.pressure.explain: Useful for tyre pressures, which are quoted in bar in Europe and psi in the US. These are gauge pressures, measured relative to the surrounding air.
chart.multiplication.title: Multiplication Table
chart.multiplication.explain: Find one factor in the left column and the other in the header; their intersection is the product. For example, row 6 and column 8 give 48. Swapping the factors gives the same result, so the grid mirrors itself across the diagonal. The table covers whole-number factors from 1 to 12. It is a multiplication lookup, not an addition table; division reverses the question only when the divisor is nonzero. Use the filter to locate displayed products, or clear it to restore the full grid.
chart.squares.title: Squares and Cubes Table
chart.squares.desc: Squares, cubes and square roots from 1 to 25.
chart.squares.explain: For each whole number n from 1 to 25, the next columns show n × n, n × n × n and the positive square root of n. At n = 4 these are 16, 64 and 2. Square roots are displayed to four decimal places, so a value such as 1.4142 for the square root of 2 is rounded, not exact. A square area of 16 square units has side length 4 units; this is different from taking the square root of the row label itself. Negative numbers and complex roots are outside this reference.
chart.primes.title: Prime Numbers Table
chart.primes.explain: This list contains the 95 primes below 500. A prime is a whole number greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. One is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime. The list is generated with the sieve of Eratosthenes, marking multiples from each prime squared. The position column counts entries in the list; it is not another prime value. To check a number not listed here, use the prime checker. For a manual check of 97, testing the primes 2, 3, 5 and 7 is sufficient because its square root is less than 10.
chart.roman.title: Roman Numeral Chart
chart.roman.desc: Roman numerals for the numbers that come up most.
chart.roman.explain: Read standard Roman numerals in groups. XLIX is XL + IX = 40 + 9 = 49; MCMXCIV is 1000 + 900 + 90 + 4 = 1994. The standard subtractive pairs are IV, IX, XL, XC, CD and CM, so a smaller symbol cannot be placed before just any larger symbol. This chart contains selected common values and years rather than every integer between its first and last entries. Use the Roman numeral tool for another value. Historical inscriptions can use different conventions; this reference uses modern subtractive notation.
chart.prefixes.title: Metric Prefixes Table
chart.prefixes.desc: SI prefixes from tera down to pico.
chart.prefixes.explain: Each prefix is a fixed power of ten. Data storage is the common exception: there, binary prefixes such as kibi and mebi count in 1024s instead.
chart.percentFraction.title: Percentage to Fraction Table
chart.percentFraction.desc: Common fractions as decimals and percentages.
chart.percentFraction.explain: Each row expresses the same proportion as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage. Divide the numerator by the denominator, then multiply the decimal by 100 for the percentage: 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5%. Recurring values are rounded for display; 1/3 is not exactly 33.33%. A percentage is dimensionless, so 12.5% of 80 is 0.125 × 80 = 10 regardless of the currency or measurement unit. To turn a percentage back into a decimal, divide by 100 rather than multiplying again.
chart.compound.title: Compound Growth Table
chart.compound.desc: What one unit of money grows to at different rates and terms.
chart.compound.explain: Each cell is a growth factor for one initial unit, with the stated annual rate compounded once a year: factor = (1 + rate/100)^years. At 5% for 10 years the factor is about 1.63; multiply your starting amount by the unrounded factor to estimate its future value. A starting amount of 100 therefore grows to about 162.89, rather than exactly 163. The table assumes a constant rate and reinvestment, with no additional deposits, withdrawals, fees, tax or inflation adjustment. These are hypothetical scenarios, not market returns or guaranteed investment outcomes.
chart.compound.note: Each figure is what 1 unit of any currency grows to, so multiply by your own starting amount. Annual compounding, no fees or tax.
chart.amortisation.title: Amortisation Schedule Example
chart.amortisation.desc: How a loan balance falls year by year.
chart.amortisation.explain: This worked loan example uses principal 100000, a fixed nominal annual rate of 5% divided into monthly rates, 240 equal end-of-month payments and no fees or payment holidays. The monthly payment is about 659.96. Each payment first covers that month of interest on the outstanding balance; the rest reduces principal. As the balance falls, the interest share falls and the principal share rises. The annual table rounds displayed amounts to whole units, so displayed totals can differ slightly from calculations using the underlying values. The figures are an arithmetic illustration, not a lender offer, APR or a local lending-rule calculation.
chart.amortisation.note: Example: {principal} borrowed at {rate} over {years} years, giving a payment of {payment} a month. Use the mortgage calculator for your own figures.
chart.inflation.title: Inflation Reference Table
chart.inflation.desc: What 100 units of today's money will still buy.
chart.inflation.explain: Each cell uses purchasing power = 100 ÷ (1 + annual inflation rate ÷ 100)^years. At 3% for 10 years, 100 ÷ 1.03^10 is about 74.41, so money held without interest buys about 25.59% less. To calculate the future price of something costing 100 today, multiply by 1.03^10 instead: about 134.39. These are inverse questions. The rates are hypothetical constant scenarios, not historical inflation data or a forecast for a particular country. The table ignores interest, investment returns, tax and changing annual rates. Use the inflation calculator for another starting amount or term, and a relevant official price index when measuring actual past inflation.
chart.inflation.note: Each figure is what 100 units of today's money buys after that many years at that rate.
chart.cooking.title: Cooking Measurement Table
chart.cooking.explain: These are US customary volume measures. One US cup is about 236.59 ml, so two cups are about 473.18 ml; displayed figures are rounded after conversion. This does not make a cup of every ingredient weigh the same: flour, sugar and oil have different densities, and packing changes dry-ingredient volume. Use a mass measurement when a recipe gives grams; a volume converter cannot infer ingredient density. An Australian tablespoon and an imperial fluid ounce differ from the US measures used here. Check the recipe’s stated measurement system before substituting a cup, spoon or pint. The linked volume converter supports other quantities, but does not convert an ingredient’s volume into its weight.
chart.cooking.note: US customary measures. An imperial or Australian tablespoon is a different size, so check which one a recipe means.
chart.paper.title: Paper Sizes Table
chart.paper.desc: A-series and US paper sizes in millimetres and inches.
chart.paper.explain: Dimensions describe the physical sheet, with the shorter side first; they are not printer resolution or the printable area. Convert millimetres to inches by dividing by exactly 25.4: A4 is 210 × 297 mm, approximately 8.27 × 11.69 inches. Portrait and landscape exchange the two sides without changing the sheet. A-series sizes retain approximately the same shape when halved; US Letter and Legal have different proportions. Scaling an A4 document to Letter therefore may leave margins or crop content. Use the printer preview to check the chosen sheet, orientation, margins and scaling; a 100% setting preserves physical dimensions only if the printer and document settings agree.
chart.paper.note: A-series dimensions are exact; US sizes are given in millimetres converted from their inch definitions.
chart.screens.title: Screen Resolution Table
chart.screens.desc: Common resolutions with aspect ratios and megapixels.
chart.screens.explain: Multiply width by height to count pixels; divide by 1,000,000 for megapixels. For Full HD, 1,920 × 1,080 = 2,073,600 pixels, or about 2.1 MP after rounding. The aspect ratio reduces width and height by their greatest common divisor, which explains the exact 683:384 ratio for 1,366 × 768. Doubling both dimensions quadruples the pixel count: 4K UHD has four times as many pixels as Full HD. More pixels do not by themselves establish physical screen size, sharpness, refresh rate, colour quality or performance. Pixel density also needs the screen diagonal; uncompressed storage also needs colour depth and frame count. The linked data converter changes storage units, not image dimensions or compression.

guide.loan-payment.title: How to Calculate a Loan Payment
guide.loan-payment.desc: The formula behind a monthly loan payment, worked through with real numbers.
guide.loan-payment.intro.1: A level-payment loan charges interest on whatever you still owe, then takes a fixed amount off each month. The payment has to be large enough to cover that month's interest and still chip away at the balance, and it has to be the same every month until the loan clears.
guide.loan-payment.intro.2: That constraint is what produces the formula below. It looks awkward, but it is just the payment that makes the balance land on exactly zero at the end of the term.
guide.loan-payment.var.payment: The monthly payment you are solving for.
guide.loan-payment.var.amount: The amount borrowed, after any deposit.
guide.loan-payment.var.rate: The monthly interest rate: the annual rate divided by 12, as a decimal.
guide.loan-payment.var.periods: The number of monthly payments, so years times 12.
guide.loan-payment.step.1: Convert the annual rate to a monthly one by dividing by 12, then by 100 to make it a decimal. A 6% loan gives 0.005.
guide.loan-payment.step.2: Count the payments. A 25-year loan paid monthly is 300 payments.
guide.loan-payment.step.3: Work out (1 + i)ⁿ - the growth factor over the whole term. This is the part a calculator is genuinely useful for.
guide.loan-payment.step.4: Put the numbers into the formula. The result is the payment that clears the loan exactly on schedule.
guide.loan-payment.example.intro: A 200,000 loan at 6% over 25 years, in whatever currency you like - the arithmetic is the same.
guide.loan-payment.note.1: The total paid over 25 years is about 386,581 - so the interest costs more than 90% of the amount borrowed again. That is the number worth looking at when comparing terms, not the monthly payment alone.
guide.loan-payment.note.2: This assumes the rate never changes. On a variable or tracker rate the payment is recalculated whenever the rate moves, so treat the result as the payment at today's rate rather than a fixed commitment.
guide.loan-payment.faq.1.q: Why is the formula not just the amount divided by the months, plus interest?
guide.loan-payment.faq.1.a: Because the interest is charged on the balance, and the balance falls every month. A fixed share of interest would overcharge at the end, when far less is owed.
guide.loan-payment.faq.2.q: What happens if I pay more than the payment?
guide.loan-payment.faq.2.a: The extra goes straight to the balance. Since interest is charged on the balance, every unit you overpay also removes all the interest that would have accrued on it for the rest of the term.
guide.compound.title: How to Calculate Compound Interest
guide.compound.desc: The compound interest formula, and what each part of it does.
guide.compound.intro.1: Simple interest pays you on what you originally put in. Compound interest pays you on the interest as well, so each period starts from a slightly larger number than the last.
guide.compound.intro.2: How often that happens matters. The same annual rate compounded monthly beats the same rate compounded yearly, because the interest starts earning sooner.
guide.compound.var.final: The final amount, including the original sum.
guide.compound.var.rate: The annual rate as a decimal: 6% is 0.06.
guide.compound.var.frequency: How many times a year interest is added.
guide.compound.step.1: Divide the annual rate by the compounding frequency. That is the rate applied each period.
guide.compound.step.2: Multiply the frequency by the years to get the number of periods.
guide.compound.step.3: Raise (1 + period rate) to that power and multiply by the starting amount.
guide.compound.example.intro: 10,000 at 6% a year, compounded monthly, for 10 years.
guide.compound.note.1: Compounded yearly instead of monthly, the same deposit reaches about 17,908 - roughly 286 less. The rate is identical; only the timing changed.
guide.compound.faq.1.a: Dividing 72 by the interest rate gives a rough number of years for money to double. At 6% that is about 12 years, and the real answer is 11.9 - close enough for mental arithmetic.
guide.compound.faq.2.q: Does this account for tax or fees?
guide.compound.faq.2.a: No. Both reduce the effective rate, so the honest way to use the formula is to put your after-tax, after-fee rate into it rather than the headline one.
guide.percentage.title: How to Calculate a Percentage
guide.percentage.desc: Percentage of a value, percentage change, and why the two are not the same.
guide.percentage.intro.1: A percentage is just a fraction with 100 on the bottom. The difficulty is almost never the arithmetic - it is that several different questions all get called “percentage”.
guide.percentage.intro.2: The most error-prone one is percentage change, because the answer depends on which number you start from. Going from 80 to 100 is a 25% increase, but going from 100 back to 80 is a 20% decrease.
guide.percentage.var.old: The starting value - the one you are measuring from.
guide.percentage.step.1: Subtract the old value from the new one to get the difference.
guide.percentage.step.2: Divide that difference by the old value, not the new one.
guide.percentage.note.1: A rise and a fall of the same percentage do not cancel out. Lose 50% and you need a 100% gain to get back, because the second percentage is taken from a smaller base.
guide.percentage.faq.1.q: What is the difference between percent and percentage points?
guide.percentage.faq.1.a: If a rate goes from 4% to 5%, that is a rise of one percentage point but a 25% increase. Reports use whichever sounds more dramatic, so it is worth checking which is meant.
guide.percentage.faq.2.q: How do I reverse a percentage increase?
guide.percentage.faq.2.a: Divide rather than subtract. To remove a 20% increase, divide by 1.20 - subtracting 20% would take off too much, because it would be 20% of the larger number.
guide.vat.title: How to Calculate VAT
guide.vat.desc: Adding VAT to a price, and working it back out of one.
guide.vat.intro.1: Adding VAT is straightforward: multiply by one plus the rate. Removing it is where people go wrong, because subtracting the rate from the gross price takes off too much.
guide.vat.intro.2: The reason is that the tax was calculated on the net price, not the gross one. 20% of the net is less than 20% of the gross, so reversing it means dividing, not subtracting.
guide.vat.var.rate: The tax rate as a decimal: 20% is 0.20.
guide.vat.step.1: To add tax, multiply the net price by one plus the rate.
guide.vat.step.2: To remove it, divide the gross price by one plus the rate. The tax is the difference.
guide.vat.note.1: Subtracting 20% from 120 gives 96, which is wrong by four units. The mistake is common enough on invoices that it is worth checking the arithmetic rather than the label.
guide.vat.faq.1.a: A shortcut for pulling tax straight out of a gross price. At 20% it is 1/6, so a sixth of 120 is 20. It is the same division written differently.
guide.vat.faq.2.q: Do all goods carry the standard rate?
guide.vat.faq.2.a: No. Most countries have reduced and zero rates for things like food, books, children's clothing and public transport. The rate depends on what is sold, not on who sells it.
guide.what-compound.title: What Is Compound Interest?
guide.what-compound.desc: What compounding means, and why time matters more than rate.
guide.what-compound.intro.1: Compound interest is interest that earns interest. Put money somewhere that pays 5%, and in the second year you earn 5% on your original amount plus 5% on the first year's interest.
guide.what-compound.intro.2: Over a year or two the difference against simple interest is barely visible. Over decades it dominates everything else, which is why the number of years usually matters more than squeezing out an extra percentage point.
guide.what-compound.intro.3: The same mechanism works against you on debt. A credit card balance compounds monthly at a high rate, which is why a minimum payment can leave a balance almost unchanged for years.
guide.what-compound.note.1: Compounding frequency matters less than people expect. Going from yearly to monthly compounding at 6% adds about 0.17 percentage points of effective return; going from 10 years to 20 roughly doubles the outcome.
guide.what-compound.note.2: Inflation compounds too. A 6% return with 3% inflation is closer to 3% in real terms, and it is the real number that decides what the money will buy.
guide.what-compound.faq.1.q: Is compound interest always better than simple interest?
guide.what-compound.faq.1.a: For money you are owed, yes. For money you owe, it is the opposite: compounding is exactly what makes a long-running debt expensive.
guide.what-compound.faq.2.a: Annual percentage yield: the rate after compounding is taken into account. It lets you compare accounts that compound at different frequencies on equal terms.
guide.what-amortisation.title: What Is Amortisation?
guide.what-amortisation.desc: How a loan balance unwinds, and why early payments feel wasted.
guide.what-amortisation.intro.1: Amortisation is the process of paying a loan off in equal instalments, where each payment covers that month's interest first and puts whatever is left towards the balance.
guide.what-amortisation.intro.2: Because interest is charged on the outstanding balance, early payments are mostly interest. As the balance falls, the interest portion shrinks and the principal portion grows, so the loan clears faster and faster towards the end.
guide.what-amortisation.intro.3: The point where principal exceeds interest depends on the interest rate and remaining term. Check the principal and interest columns of your schedule rather than assuming a particular year.
guide.what-amortisation.note.1: This is why overpaying early is worth far more than overpaying late. A unit paid in year one removes 24 years of interest that would have accrued on it; the same unit in year 24 removes almost none.
guide.what-amortisation.faq.1.q: Why does my balance barely move in the first year?
guide.what-amortisation.faq.1.a: Because the balance is at its highest, so the interest charged is at its highest too. Most of the payment is covering that interest rather than reducing what you owe.
guide.what-amortisation.faq.2.a: No. An interest-only payment covers the interest and nothing else, so the balance stays where it is until you repay it some other way.
guide.what-inflation.title: What Is Inflation?
guide.what-inflation.desc: What inflation does to money that is not doing anything.
guide.what-inflation.intro.1: Inflation is a general rise in prices, which is the same thing as a fall in what a unit of money buys. If prices rise 3% this year, the same note buys about 3% less than it did.
guide.what-inflation.intro.2: It compounds, exactly like interest. At 3% a year, money loses about a quarter of its purchasing power over a decade and around 45% over twenty years.
guide.what-inflation.intro.3: This is why a long-term plan has to be stated in real terms. A retirement target that looks generous in today's money can be uncomfortable by the time you reach it.
guide.what-inflation.note.1: Your personal inflation rate is not the headline one. The published figure is an average across a basket of goods; if your spending is weighted towards rent or energy, your experience can be very different.
guide.what-inflation.faq.1.q: What is the difference between nominal and real returns?
guide.what-inflation.faq.1.a: Nominal is the number quoted; real is what is left after inflation. A 5% return with 3% inflation is about 2% real, and it is the real figure that decides what you can buy.
guide.what-inflation.faq.2.a: Not usually. Falling prices sound good for savers, but they encourage people to delay spending, which reduces demand and tends to make debt harder to repay.
guide.what-marginal.title: What Is a Marginal Tax Rate?
guide.what-marginal.desc: Why moving into a higher tax bracket does not cut your take-home pay.
guide.what-marginal.intro.1: Your marginal rate is the rate charged on your next unit of income. Your effective rate is the total tax divided by your total income. They are almost never the same number.
guide.what-marginal.intro.2: That is because tax bands are sliced, not switched. Income inside each band is taxed at that band's rate; only the part above a threshold pays the higher rate.
guide.what-marginal.intro.3: So earning one unit more never leaves you worse off overall. The extra unit is taxed more heavily, but everything below the threshold carries on being taxed exactly as before.
guide.what-marginal.note.1: There are real exceptions, and they come from benefits and allowances rather than the bands themselves - a tapered allowance or a withdrawn credit can create a spike in the effective marginal rate over a narrow range of income.
guide.what-marginal.faq.1.q: Will a pay rise push me into a higher bracket and cost me money?
guide.what-marginal.faq.1.a: Not from the bands alone. Only the income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so more gross pay always means more net pay.
guide.what-marginal.faq.2.q: Which rate should I use for a decision?
guide.what-marginal.faq.2.a: The marginal rate, for anything that changes your income at the edges - a bonus, overtime, or a pension contribution. The effective rate is for understanding the total bill.
guide.compare-loans.title: How to Compare Loan Offers
guide.compare-loans.desc: What to compare when two offers have different rates and terms.
guide.compare-loans.intro.1: A lower monthly payment is not a cheaper loan. Stretching the same amount over more years reduces the payment and increases the total interest, often substantially.
guide.compare-loans.intro.2: Comparing properly means holding one thing constant and looking at the total cost rather than the instalment.
guide.compare-loans.step.1: Work out the total paid for each offer: the monthly payment multiplied by the number of payments, plus any arrangement fee.
guide.compare-loans.step.2: Compare like terms. If one offer is over 20 years and another over 25, recalculate both over the same period before deciding.
guide.compare-loans.step.3: Check what the rate is fixed for. A low rate fixed for two years on a 25-year loan is a two-year price, not a 25-year one.
guide.compare-loans.step.4: Look at early repayment terms. A loan you can overpay freely is worth more than its rate suggests.
guide.compare-loans.note.1: Advertised APR helps because it folds in compulsory fees, but it still assumes you keep the loan for the full term. If you expect to repay early, model that instead.
guide.compare-loans.faq.1.q: Is a shorter term always better?
guide.compare-loans.faq.1.a: It always costs less in total, but it costs more each month. The right term is the shortest one whose payment you can sustain without relying on everything going well.
guide.read-schedule.title: How to Read an Amortisation Schedule
guide.read-schedule.desc: What each column means and what to look for.
guide.read-schedule.intro.1: An amortisation schedule lists every payment over the life of a loan, split into the part that covers interest and the part that reduces the balance.
guide.read-schedule.intro.2: It is the most honest document about a loan, because it shows where the money actually goes rather than what the monthly figure looks like.
guide.read-schedule.step.1: Start with the interest column. Its total is the real price of borrowing; compare it to the amount borrowed.
guide.read-schedule.step.2: Find the crossover: the first row where the principal portion exceeds the interest portion. On a long loan it arrives later than expected.
guide.read-schedule.step.3: Check the balance column against the halfway point of the term. On a 25-year loan at typical rates, well over half the balance is still outstanding at year 12.
guide.read-schedule.note.1: A schedule assumes the rate never changes and every payment lands on time. It is a model of the loan, not a record of it.
guide.read-schedule.faq.1.q: Why does the last payment differ slightly?
guide.read-schedule.faq.1.a: Rounding. Each payment is rounded to the nearest minor unit, and the final one absorbs the accumulated difference so the balance lands exactly on zero.
guide.plan-savings.title: How to Plan Monthly Savings
guide.plan-savings.desc: Turning a goal and a date into a monthly number.
guide.plan-savings.intro.1: Most savings plans fail because they start from what is left over rather than from the target. Working backwards from the goal gives a number you can actually check against.
guide.plan-savings.intro.2: The arithmetic is the future value formula rearranged: given the target, the time and the expected return, solve for the contribution.
guide.plan-savings.step.1: Write down the target and the date. A goal without a date has no monthly number attached to it.
guide.plan-savings.step.2: Subtract what you already have, grown at your expected rate. That is the shortfall the contributions have to cover.
guide.plan-savings.step.3: Divide the shortfall by the annuity factor for your rate and term - or let the planner do it, which is what it is for.
guide.plan-savings.note.1: For anything under about three years, assume no return at all. Markets are volatile over short periods, and a plan that needs a good year to work is not a plan.
guide.plan-savings.faq.1.q: Should I save or repay debt first?
guide.plan-savings.faq.1.a: Compare the rates. Debt costing more than your savings earn is worth clearing first - though keeping a small buffer prevents the next surprise turning into new debt.
guide.fv.title: The Future Value Formula
guide.fv.desc: What regular contributions grow into, and why the formula has that shape.
guide.fv.intro.1: Every contribution you make compounds for a different length of time: the first one grows for the whole term, the last one for a single period. The future value formula adds all of those up in one step rather than month by month.
guide.fv.var.fv: The value of all contributions at the end.
guide.fv.var.contribution: The amount paid in each period.
guide.fv.var.rate: The rate per period - the annual rate divided by the number of periods.
guide.fv.step.1: Convert the annual rate to a per-period rate.
guide.fv.step.2: Count the contributions: years times contributions per year.
guide.fv.step.3: Apply the formula. The trailing (1 + i) is there because each contribution is made at the start of the period, so it earns one extra period of growth.
guide.fv.example.intro: 500 a month for 20 years at 7% a year.
guide.fv.note.1: Of that total, 120,000 is money paid in and the rest is growth. The split shifts heavily towards growth the longer the term runs, which is the whole argument for starting early.
guide.fv.faq.1.q: Why does my bank's figure differ slightly?
guide.fv.faq.1.a: Usually timing. This version assumes contributions at the start of each period; if yours are taken at the end, drop the trailing (1 + i) and the result falls by one period of growth.
